name: Yara Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a big wheel loader at a phosphate mine, at the rail loadout, which is where the ore gets loaded onto trains. A train comes in with a hundred and twenty wagons, and I fill the bins that feed them, steady and even so no wagon is overloaded. I'm the senior operator on the loadout, so I also plan the shift around the train timetable and sort out the young ones when they panic. I like the rhythm of it, the train creeping forward and everything flowing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's life like outside the mine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Busy. My husband Karim and I own half of an earthmoving business that our two sons run, digging house sites and farm dams with three excavators and a tip truck. I do the books and the quoting at night, and I use AI for all of it, every day: quotes, invoices, even working out the fuel. I'm fifty-eight, I've been at the mine twenty-seven years, and I'm not slowing down yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but useful. It saved me hours on the books, so I'm not complaining. I'd say that at work and in the local business owners' group online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a bit disappointing. I'd been planning for bigger changes, at the mine and in the business. But it's a safe picture, and we'd do fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Keep the AI tools for the business, keep working at the mine for another four or five years, keep helping the boys grow the business. Maybe buy a fourth excavator next year, as we'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you start using AI for the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger son Omar set it up, but I took to it straight away. I used to spend Sunday nights on quotes. Now I describe the job, check the numbers and send it before dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the mine that would change, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The train scheduling, probably. A program could plan the loading better than the whiteboard we use now. That'd be fine by me.

S0.say: I'd say it was overhyped but useful, because it saved me hours on the business books. I'd say it at work and in the local business owners' group online.
S0.think: Privately it's a bit disappointing, since I'd planned for bigger changes at the mine and in the business. But it's a safe picture and we'd be fine.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools for the family earthmoving business and keeps working at the mine for four or five more years. Buys a fourth excavator next year as planned.
S0.quote: I used to spend Sunday nights on quotes. Now I describe the job, check the numbers and send it before dinner.
S0.fieldNote: Yara is both a senior miner and a business owner, and she thinks like the latter. She already uses AI daily for the family business. Her mild disappointment in a calm picture shows how ready she is for change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity, if you're willing to work. The people who learn the new tools will do well. I'd say it at work and to the boys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the business is the bigger story than the mine. If excavators get smarter, a small firm like ours can do more with fewer people. At the mine, I'd probably finish my time running a train loadout that's partly automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at buying a semi-automated excavator for the business, one that can follow a digital plan on its own, once the price came down. I'd volunteer for any automation training at the mine, because I'd learn things I could use in the business. And I'd keep putting money back into the business rather than spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd bring automation into your own business. Would that cost anyone a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe one operator, eventually. But right now we turn down work because we can't find people. A smarter machine means we say yes to more jobs, not fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the boys think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Omar would love it, he's the techie one. Yusuf, the older one, is old-fashioned, he'd say a machine can't feel the ground. He's right, but it can follow a plan better than a tired person at four o'clock.

S1.say: I'd say it's an opportunity for anyone willing to work, and those who learn the new tools will do well. I'd say it at work and to my sons.
S1.think: Privately I think the business matters more than the mine, because smarter excavators let a small firm do more with fewer people. At the mine I'd finish my time on a partly automated loadout.
S1.do: Plans to buy a semi-automated excavator for the business once prices fall. Volunteers for automation training at the mine and reinvests money in the business.
S1.quote: A smarter machine means we say yes to more jobs, not fewer people.
S1.fieldNote: Yara sees Steady Disruption mainly through her family business, where automation could solve a labour shortage. She is practical about the job effect and doesn't pretend it's zero. The contrast between her two sons gave a nice picture of family debate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get ready, because it's here. Families and small businesses need to move fast, and nobody's going to do it for us. I'd say it in the business group and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried about the business more than the mine. If big firms get robot excavators in two years, they could undercut us on every job, and we'd be stuck with three old machines worth half what we paid. My own savings are fine, but the boys' livelihoods are in that business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the mine within the first year and work on the business full-time, because that's where I'd be needed. I'd sell one of the older excavators while it still had value and put that money towards an automated one. I'd sit down with the boys and look at moving into jobs robots won't want yet, like small repairs and tricky sites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicked, but my head would be full of numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the two-year timeline change things for the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years, we'd be racing the big companies with less money and less time. With five or ten, we could save up, buy at the right time and grow into it. Two years forces us to bet before we're ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the boys that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, nobody's coming to save us, so we work it out ourselves, as a family. Then I'd open the laptop and start running numbers. Karim would make tea and tell us all to go to bed.

S2.say: I'd say get ready because it's here, and families and small businesses need to move fast because nobody will do it for us. I'd say it in the business group and at work.
S2.think: Privately I'm more worried about the business than the mine, since big firms with robot excavators could undercut us and leave our machines worth half. My savings are fine, but my sons' livelihoods are in that business.
S2.do: Leaves the mine within the first year to work on the family business full-time. Sells an older excavator while it holds value to fund an automated one, and plans with her sons to move into jobs robots won't want yet.
S2.feel: Uneasy but not panicked, with her head full of numbers.
S2.quote: Two years forces us to bet before we're ready.
S2.fieldNote: For Yara the threat runs through the family business, not her mine job or savings. She responds with self-reliance and quick action, consistent with her traditional and adaptive mix. She would leave the mine without hesitation if the family needed her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to get ahead of it, if you start now. Learn the tools, invest wisely, and don't wait for government. I'd say it to anyone in business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's a good amount of time. I'd be sixty-three, ready to leave the mine anyway. The business would have time to change its machines and its kind of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the mine for two or three more years and put most of my pay into the business. We'd buy one automated excavator around 2028, once the first models had a track record, and use it on the big subdivision jobs. Then I'd leave the mine and help the boys full-time on the planning and quoting side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years give you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives us time to buy one machine, learn it, and make our mistakes on our own jobs before the big firms get there. That's worth a lot. In two years, our first mistake might be our last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you worry about your own job at the mine in those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Somebody still has to run the loadout until the new system's proven, and I'd happily help train it. If they offered me a package early, I'd take it and put it into the business.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if you start now, learning the tools, investing wisely and not waiting for government. I'd say it to anyone in business.
S3.think: Privately it's a good amount of time, since I'd be sixty-three and ready to leave the mine. The business would have time to change its machines and its kind of work.
S3.do: Works two or three more years at the mine and puts most of her pay into the business. Buys an automated excavator around 2028 once early models prove themselves, then leaves the mine to help with planning and quoting.
S3.quote: In two years, our first mistake might be our last.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Yara plan the business shift calmly, buying one machine and learning on her own jobs. She is unbothered about her mine job and would take an early package to fund the business. Her focus on self-reliance is steady throughout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so anyone who isn't ready has only themselves to blame. Plan, save, learn. I'd say that to the young people at the mine and at the mosque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's comfortable. I'd be retired from the mine and helping the boys part-time. The business would have ten years to grow into the new machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd retire from the mine around sixty-two and step back into a part-time role in the business. We'd change the fleet over slowly, one machine every couple of years. And I'd help Omar do a course in machine control and surveying, so he's the one running the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Good, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the ten-year picture that bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people might get lazy with ten years' notice and not prepare. I've seen it before, with the old processing plant closing. Everyone knew for five years and half the town still acted surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell young people at the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands and something with a computer. Either one alone won't be enough. And save money, because the people who did well when the plant closed were the ones with something in the bank.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so anyone not ready has only themselves to blame. I'd tell young people at the mine and at the mosque to plan, save and learn.
S4.think: Privately it's comfortable, since I'd be retired from the mine and helping my sons part-time. The business would have ten years to grow into the new machines.
S4.do: Retires from the mine around 62 and steps into a part-time role in the business. Changes the fleet over one machine every couple of years and helps Omar take a course in machine control and surveying.
S4.quote: Everyone knew for five years and half the town still acted surprised.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Yara is entirely relaxed and focused on steady fleet renewal and her son's training. Her story about the processing plant closure shapes her belief that preparation is a personal responsibility. Faith and family appear as natural parts of her life rather than talking points.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the business wouldn't have time to switch over and the big firms would eat us. What would help is the banks lending to small family businesses to buy the new machines, at fair rates, so it's not just the big companies who can afford them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about small businesses. Everyone thinks about workers and big companies. But in towns like ours, it's family firms with three machines that do half the work, and we need a fair chance at the new technology too.

headlineQuote: In towns like ours, it's family firms with three machines that do half the work, and we need a fair chance at the new technology too.
portrait: Yara Farah is a 58-year-old senior wheel loader operator at a phosphate mine's rail loadout who also co-owns a family earthmoving business run by her two sons, handling its books with AI every day. She is secure, self-reliant and curious, and sees most of the pictures as an opportunity for the business rather than a threat to her mine job. She is calm in the slower pictures and uneasy only in AGI by 2028, when big firms with robot excavators could undercut the family business before it can adapt. She believes families and businesses must prepare themselves rather than wait for government, and wants fair access to finance for small firms.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the family business wouldn't have time to switch over before big firms undercut it.
whatWouldHelp: Banks lending to small family businesses at fair rates so they can buy the new automated machines, not only big companies.
